arguments.title: March 2023 Board-Framing Case Study: Financing Miss vs. Execution
arguments.body:
## The distinction

In March 2023, we framed the missed round as a financing-market outcome—not as evidence that the team had failed to execute. The product and team had met the commitments set for them; investor timing, frozen buyers, and tightening budgets made the round unavailable on terms we would accept.

## What the board heard

We avoided both blame-shifting and false self-criticism. Instead, we proposed a disciplined bridge: show the amount, months of runway, and milestones it funded; hold hiring tighter, keep engineering focused on launch-critical work, and defer speculative GTM experiments. The Q3 launch—not a vague promise of more time—was the next proof point investors could underwrite.

## What we did not overclaim

Execution was not presented as flawless. Directors were right to challenge the retention story: the available view blended sources and obscured cohort detail. We called that a data gap, committed to a sharper month-12 cohort cut (including a sensitivity excluding the largest early customer), and kept the bridge case separate from that unresolved operating evidence.

## Why the framing mattered

It made the decision legible: the financing miss changed the company’s cash and spending posture, but did not retroactively turn delivered work into an execution failure. At the same time, naming the retention evidence gap kept the explanation credible and gave the board a concrete follow-up.
